scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Cheerleading in the United Kingdom has grown into a widespread competitive sport encompassing over 89,000 athletes, with more than 900 teams based in England alone.
The discipline is practiced primarily through private all-star clubs, alongside school physical education programs and university squads.
By 2018, 70 British universities offered cheerleading as an extracurricular activity, with 23 participating competitively.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Cheerleading in the United Kingdom is practiced primarily as a competitive sport and extracurricular athletic pursuit rather than sideline support.

Events range from regional school and university tournaments to national championship qualifiers where teams compete for bids to international events such as the ICU World Championships and IASF Worlds.
The discipline also emphasizes inclusivity, having established foundational divisions for athletes with physical and intellectual impairments.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Rick Rodgers, a disabled British athlete, founded ParaCheer International and collaborated with the ICU to establish the Adaptive Abilities division.
Unity Allstars' squad Ruby was featured in an Olympic Channel 10-minute documentary highlighting UK competitive cheerleading.
Cheerleading operates throughout England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, and the Isle of Man under their respective home-nation bodies within SportCheer UK.

Cheerleading in the United Kingdom operates as a recognized branch of the global cheerleading movement governed by the International Cheer Union (ICU) and the International All Star Federation (IASF).
